title: First Missing Positive
approach_name: Place each positive value at its matching index
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the smallest missing positive integer in an unsorted array, with O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The answer must be between 1 and n+1.
Idea: For every value x in [1,n], swap it toward index x-1 until that position already holds x or the value is out of range. Then find the first mismatched index.
Technique and why it applies: In-place index placement uses the array itself to represent membership without a separate set.
Invariant: Whenever a value x in [1,n] is correctly placed, nums[x-1] equals x and remains there.
Edge cases: Ignore zero, negatives, and values above n. Duplicate values must not cause an endless swap loop.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each successful swap places a value correctly. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each successful swap permanently places a value in its target slot.

title: Trapping Rain Water
notes:
Task and constraints: Each non-negative height represents a bar of width one. Compute the total water retained between bars; water at a position is limited by the smaller of its left and right maximum heights.
Idea: Move two pointers inward while tracking leftMax and rightMax. Process the side with the smaller current boundary, since that side's water level is already determined.
Technique and why it applies: The smaller boundary limits trapped water, and the opposite side can only help if it is at least as high.
Invariant: Every processed position has a known limiting maximum and its trapped contribution is added exactly once.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three cannot trap water. Equal boundary heights can be processed from either side.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each pointer advances once per iteration. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The two boundaries move inward and only a few maximums and the total are stored.

title: Multiply Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: Multiply two non-negative integers represented as decimal strings without converting the full strings to machine integers or using BigInteger.
Idea: Allocate an array of length m+n. Multiply each digit pair and add the partial product into positions i+j and i+j+1, propagating carry through the result array.
Technique and why it applies: Ordinary long multiplication decomposes the product into digit products, and the result array stores each decimal place independently.
Invariant: After processing a digit pair, its product and carry are reflected in the corresponding result positions.
Edge cases: If either input is "0", return "0". Strip leading zeroes from the final representation but preserve one zero if the product is zero.
Complexity: Time is O(mn) for every digit pair. Extra space is O(m+n) for the digit array and output.
complexity_reason: The digit array has m+n positions and each digit pair is multiplied once.

title: Wildcard Matching
approach_name: DP for string and wildcard prefixes
notes:
Task and constraints: Match the entire string against a pattern where '?' matches exactly one character and '*' matches any sequence, including the empty sequence.
Idea: Define dp[i][j] for whether the first i input characters match the first j pattern characters. A normal character or '?' uses the diagonal state; '*' either consumes no input or extends a match by one character.
Technique and why it applies: Each wildcard has a precise prefix transition, so a table can build answers from shorter prefixes.
Invariant: Every filled cell accurately records full matching for its two prefixes.
Edge cases: Leading stars can match an empty input, so initialize the first DP row accordingly. Matching must consume both full strings.
Complexity: Time and space are O(mn) for the table of prefix pairs.
complexity_reason: Each string-pattern prefix pair is computed once.

title: Jump Game II
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of jumps from index zero to the final index; each element gives the maximum jump distance. The input guarantees reachability.
Idea: Track the end of the current jump range and the farthest index reachable from any position in that range. When the scan reaches the current range end, commit one jump and advance the range.
Technique and why it applies: Every index in a range is reachable with the same number of jumps; the farthest reach defines the next range and greedily maximizes progress.
Invariant: farthest is the maximum reachable index seen in the current layer, and jumps counts the minimum jumps needed to reach the current layer.
Edge cases: A single-element array needs zero jumps. Do not count a jump until the current layer boundary is reached.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: A single scan maintains three indices/counters.

title: Permutations
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all permutations of an array of distinct integers. Each result uses every input element exactly once.
Idea: Build a path by selecting any unused value, recurse, and undo the selection after the recursive call returns.
Technique and why it applies: A permutation is an ordering of all elements, so branching on the next unused value enumerates every possible ordering exactly once.
Invariant: The path contains distinct selected values and used marks exactly those values; at full length it is a complete permutation.
Edge cases: A one-element array produces one permutation. The empty array convention yields one empty permutation, though the stated constraints are non-empty.
Complexity: Time is O(n·n!) because n! results of length n are materialized. Auxiliary recursion/path space is O(n), excluding output.
complexity_reason: There are n! permutations and each is copied with n elements.

title: Permutations II
notes:
Task and constraints: Return each distinct permutation of an array that may contain repeated values. The answer must not contain duplicate arrangements.
Idea: Sort the array, then backtrack with a used-index array. At a recursion level, skip a value equal to its predecessor when that predecessor has not been used in the current path.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting groups equal values together; the same-depth check prevents equivalent branches while still allowing identical values to occupy separate positions in one permutation.
Invariant: The path uses each index at most once, and only the first available equal value is chosen as a sibling branch.
Edge cases: Repeated values can appear multiple times in one permutation. The skip condition must include not used[i-1].
Complexity: Worst-case time is O(n·n!) and auxiliary recursion space is O(n), excluding output.
complexity_reason: Each recursion level tries unused values, skipping duplicate sibling branches.

title: Rotate Image
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place; no second matrix may be allocated.
Idea: First transpose across the main diagonal by swapping matrix[r][c] with matrix[c][r], then reverse each row.
Technique and why it applies: Transposition maps coordinates (r,c) to (c,r), and reversing columns maps the result to the required clockwise coordinate transformation.
Invariant: After transposition, rows and columns have exchanged; row reversal completes the clockwise rotation while preserving all values.
Edge cases: A 1x1 matrix remains unchanged. Transpose only pairs with c greater than r to avoid undoing swaps.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) because each cell participates in constant work. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The matrix is transformed in place with swaps only.

title: Group Anagrams
notes:
Task and constraints: Group strings that contain the same characters with the same frequencies. The order of groups and members within groups is unrestricted.
Idea: Sort the characters of each string to form a canonical key, then append the original string to the list associated with that key.
Technique and why it applies: Anagrams have identical sorted character sequences, so the key groups exactly the strings with the same multiset of letters.
Invariant: Every string is stored in the group for its canonical key, and no string is dropped.
Edge cases: Empty strings share the empty key. Different lengths cannot be anagrams because their sorted keys differ.
Complexity: Time is O(k·m log m) for k strings of maximum length m. Space is O(total input characters plus output).
complexity_reason: Each string is sorted to build its canonical anagram key.

title: Pow(x, n)
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute x raised to an integer exponent n, including negative exponents, where n can be as small as -2^31.
Idea: Convert negative exponents to reciprocals, then repeatedly square the base and halve the exponent, multiplying the result whenever the current exponent is odd.
Technique and why it applies: Squaring reuses powers efficiently, reducing the number of multiplications from linear in |n| to logarithmic.
Invariant: At each step, result times base raised to the remaining exponent equals the requested power.
Edge cases: Negating the minimum 32-bit exponent overflows in Java, so widen it to long before negation. Exponent zero returns one.
Complexity: Time is O(log |n|) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The exponent is halved each iteration and only scalar values are retained.

title: N-Queens
approach_name: Place queens with column and diagonal sets
notes:
Task and constraints: Place n queens on an n x n board so no two queens share a column or diagonal, and return every distinct board. n is at most 9.
Idea: Place one queen per row. Track occupied columns and the two diagonal identifiers row-col and row+col; recurse only when all three are free.
Technique and why it applies: Row-by-row placement guarantees no shared rows, while the sets prune column and diagonal conflicts immediately.
Invariant: All queens already placed occupy distinct columns and diagonals, and each prior row has exactly one queen.
Edge cases: n=1 has one board. Each output board is built from the chosen column for every row.
Complexity: Search is exponential in n in the worst case; output space is O(number of solutions times n^2), with O(n) recursion state.
complexity_reason: The recursion stores one column per row and the sets mark occupied columns and diagonals.

title: N-Queens II
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of distinct placements of n queens on an n x n board such that no two queens attack one another. n is at most 9.
Idea: Place one queen in each row, tracking used columns and diagonals. Increment the count when all rows have been filled.
Technique and why it applies: Since every solution has exactly one queen per row, row-by-row backtracking enumerates all candidates while rejecting conflicts early.
Invariant: The partial placement has one queen in each earlier row and no shared column or diagonal.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one. The method counts solutions without constructing board strings, so it uses less output memory than N-Queens.
Complexity: Search is exponential in n in the worst case. Auxiliary space is O(n) for recursion and constraint state.
complexity_reason: Only one row's placement and three occupancy arrays/sets are retained.

title: Maximum Subarray
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray. Values may be negative, so the chosen subarray must contain at least one element.
Idea: At each value, either start a new subarray there or extend the best subarray ending at the previous index. Track the largest ending sum and the global maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Any optimal subarray ending at the current index either consists only of the current value or extends the best valid suffix ending before it.
Invariant: current is the best sum of a subarray ending at the current position; best is the maximum over all positions processed.
Edge cases: All-negative arrays must return their largest element, not zero. Initialize both values from nums[0].
Complexity: Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each value updates two running sums without storing subarray states.

title: Spiral Matrix
notes:
Task and constraints: Return every element of a rectangular matrix in clockwise spiral order. Matrix dimensions are positive and at most 10 in this problem.
Idea: Maintain top, bottom, left, and right boundaries. Traverse the top row, right column, bottom row in reverse, and left column upward, shrinking the relevant boundary after each pass.
Technique and why it applies: The unvisited cells always form a smaller rectangle after one complete perimeter is processed.
Invariant: The output contains the visited outer layers in spiral order, and the boundary rectangle contains exactly the unvisited cells.
Edge cases: Check boundaries before traversing bottom and left edges because a final row or column may have been consumed by an earlier pass.
Complexity: Time is O(mn), as every cell is appended once. Extra space is O(1) excluding the returned list.
complexity_reason: Each cell is visited once as the four boundaries shrink.

title: Jump Game
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether the final index can be reached from the first index, with each element specifying the maximum jump length from that position.
Idea: Scan from left to right while tracking the farthest index reachable from any visited position. If the scan index ever exceeds that reach, the end is unreachable.
Technique and why it applies: Every reachable position can extend the known reach, and no path can get beyond the maximum reach discovered so far.
Invariant: farthest is the greatest index reachable using any position at or before the current scan index.
Edge cases: A one-element array is already at the destination. A zero can block progress if it is exactly beyond the current reach.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: One pass updates the farthest reachable index.

title: Merge Intervals
notes:
Task and constraints: Merge intervals that overlap and return sorted, non-overlapping intervals covering the same points.
Idea: Sort by interval start. If the next interval begins at or before the last merged end, extend that end; otherwise append a new interval.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting ensures any interval that can overlap the current merged interval appears next; once a gap is found, later starts cannot bridge it from the left.
Invariant: The output intervals are sorted and pairwise non-overlapping, and they cover exactly the input intervals processed so far.
Edge cases: Touching endpoints count as overlap under the usual inclusive interval interpretation. A single interval returns itself.
Complexity: Time is O(n log n) for sorting plus a linear merge. Extra space is O(n) for the output.
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates; the merged result stores at most n intervals.

title: Insert Interval
approach_name: Append before, merge overlap, append after
notes:
Task and constraints: Insert a new interval into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and merge any intervals it overlaps.
Idea: Append intervals ending before the new interval, merge all intervals whose starts are at most the new end, then append the merged interval and the untouched suffix.
Technique and why it applies: Because input intervals are already sorted and disjoint, only a consecutive block can overlap the new interval.
Invariant: The output prefix is sorted and non-overlapping; after processing the overlap block, the new merged interval ends no earlier than every absorbed interval.
Edge cases: The new interval may overlap none, all, or the first/last intervals. Touching endpoints are merged under inclusive interval rules.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each interval is processed once. Extra space is O(n) for the output.
complexity_reason: Each input interval is appended once or absorbed into the merged interval.

title: Length of Last Word
approach_name: Scan backward over spaces and word
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the length of the final word in a string containing words and spaces. A word is a maximal run of non-space characters.
Idea: Move backward past trailing spaces, then count characters until the beginning of the string or the next space.
Technique and why it applies: The last word is a suffix after ignoring trailing spaces, so no split or list of all words is necessary.
Invariant: Once trailing spaces are skipped, the counter measures only characters belonging to the final word.
Edge cases: Leading spaces do not affect the final word length. The input contains at least one word, but trailing spaces may be present.
Complexity: Time is O(n) in the worst case. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The string is scanned backward without allocating split substrings.

title: Spiral Matrix II
approach_name: Fill shrinking boundaries in spiral order
notes:
Task and constraints: Generate an n x n matrix filled with the integers 1 through n^2 in clockwise spiral order, with n at most 20.
Idea: Maintain top, bottom, left, and right boundaries. Fill the top row, right column, bottom row, and left column in sequence, shrinking boundaries after each side.
Technique and why it applies: Each pass fills the outer perimeter of the remaining rectangle, so the next integer always goes into the next spiral position.
Invariant: All cells outside the active boundary rectangle have been filled in spiral order, and the next value is placed only inside the unfilled rectangle.
Edge cases: Check that the row and column boundaries have not crossed before filling bottom and left sides, particularly for odd n.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2), since every cell is assigned once. Space is O(n^2) for the returned matrix.

title: Permutation Sequence
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the kth permutation in lexicographic order of the numbers 1 through n, with n at most 9 and k between 1 and n!.
Idea: Convert k to zero-based indexing. At each position, factorial block sizes determine which remaining number begins the permutation; remove that number and continue with the remainder.
Technique and why it applies: Each first choice groups (n-1)! permutations, each second choice groups (n-2)! permutations, and so on, allowing direct selection without generating all permutations.
Invariant: After each choice, k identifies the rank within the permutations of the remaining unused values.
Edge cases: k is one-based in the prompt, so subtract one before using factorial division. The remaining list is ordered ascending to preserve lexicographic order.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) due to list removal and scanning. Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Factorials are precomputed in O(n), and removing each selected number from a list costs O(n).
